extracted.intended_audience: mathematics faculty, department assessment coordinators, and administrators responsible for undergraduate mathematics assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, implementing, and evaluating assessment systems for undergraduate mathematics courses, majors, and departments, including principles, purposes, and methods. Focuses on aligning goals, gathering appropriate evidence, making valid inferences, and using assessment to improve instruction and programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment is not a single event, but a continuous cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment must be a cyclic process of setting goals, selecting methods, gathering evidence, drawing inferences, taking action, and then reexamining goals and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first principle in the chapter. The assessment cycle functions as the feedback loop of education (thermostat analogy). Use the cycle for planning (why, who, what, how, when), formative monitoring (mid-course implementation and progress), and summative evaluation (recording impact and comparing outcomes with goals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with clear, appropriate goals aligned with stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment begins with goals; assessment fosters reflection on program and course goals and ensures that what is measured corresponds to what is valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether you need to measure 'temperature' (one dimension) or 'humidity' (another) — choose instruments that measure the right quantity. Involve constituencies (students, faculty, administrators, employers, public) to ensure goals are appropriate and expectations match. Without clear goals, assessment risks measuring the wrong thing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment must be an open process
rubrics_metrics.description: Goal-setting and assessment should involve diverse constituencies to ensure appropriateness and legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Involve students, faculty, administrators, parents, employers, and other stakeholders. Expect diverse and sometimes incompatible goals; value variety rather than forcing uniformity. Openness helps ensure assessment addresses the needs of multiple constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment must promote valid inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should support valid causal attributions from evidence to causes so that actions taken in response to evidence are likely to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when inferring causes of observed effects — distant effects are harder to attribute. Consider alternative explanations (e.g., low performance might be due to context, not lack of instruction). Design evidence-collection and analysis to strengthen validity of inferences before implementing corrective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple measures of performance when assessment matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment that matters should always employ multiple measures of performance because single measures are often crude or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the integrity of evidence to the consequences of decisions: informal student comments may help immediate instruction but are inappropriate for tenure decisions. Standardized diagnostics are useful for advising but may be inappropriate for blocking access to programs. Use a combination of tests, authentic tasks, portfolios, interviews, surveys, and other sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure what is worth learning, not just what is easy to measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment instruments should target the mathematical knowledge and skills that are important (including higher-order skills and contextual problem solving), not only rote calculation or what is easily scored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid focusing solely on atomized knowledge (objective items) that ignore interrelated concepts. Include authentic and performance-based tasks to assess problem-solving, communication, and contextual application. Rhetorical skill or symbolic manipulation alone are not evidence of understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match evidence quality to stakes (commensurate integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality and rigor of assessment evidence must be commensurate with the potential consequences of its use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-stakes decisions (admissions, tenure, program closure) require high-integrity evidence and procedures. Lower-stakes formative uses can rely on quicker, less formal measures. Ensure procedures (sampling, scoring) are robust when decisions have major impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure fairness and protect students' opportunity to learn
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should support every student's opportunity to learn important mathematics and be sensitive to impacts on diverse subpopulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider differential impact across ethnic groups, genders, ages, aspirations, preparation levels, and social classes. Items that are psychometrically unbiased can still have unbalanced impacts because of context or use. Avoid inappropriate uses that amplify bias and reduce equitable opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodate diversity of student goals and backgrounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment systems should recognize diverse student interests, talents, and educational backgrounds rather than enforcing uniform objectives for all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction and assessment to amplify multiple forms of mathematical talent and to serve varied needs (majors, service students, developmental learners, teacher candidates). Consensus on goals is useful but should not mask legitimate diversity of objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor formative assessment for timely improvement, use summative appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Formative assessment monitors implementation and progress during instruction and is valuable for immediate improvements; summative assessment records impact and compares outcomes with goals at the end of a course or program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions often reward late summative evaluation; prioritize timely formative evaluation to improve teaching. Use summative assessment to stimulate action (modify, extend, replicate) only after careful inference and when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of procedural traps and advocacy disguised as assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment can be distorted by institutional policies, delegation to uninvolved individuals, slanted selection of criteria, or external evaluators under promotional pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid delegating assessment to those with no instructional responsibility, and avoid selection of evaluation criteria that serve advocacy rather than objective appraisal. Design procedures to minimize incentives for delay, façade accountability, and biased reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authentic, performance-based assessments despite costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Authentic performance tasks (projects, oral exams, portfolios, presentations) better measure real mathematical ability and higher-order skills, though they are more expensive and sometimes perceived as less objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance assessments replicate real challenges and are widely used in music, athletics, and drama; apply similar approaches in mathematics when assessing contextual problem solving and communication. Be prepared for higher resource needs and address concerns about subjectivity through rubrics, multiple raters, and clear criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select assessment methods from a broad toolbox appropriate to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many valid methods for assessment — capstone courses, comprehensive exams, core exams, diagnostics, external examiners, employer feedback, focus groups, portfolios, projects, interviews, journals, oral exams, performance tasks, surveys, visiting committees, and more — and methods should be chosen to fit goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinations of methods to serve different purposes: placement, grading, program review, curriculum revision, accreditation. The book lists many specific options and illustrates how different tools align with formative vs summative purposes and with different stakes and audiences.
